explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Zechariah lifts up his eyes and sees "four chariots coming out from between two mountains—mountains of bronze." Zechariah is the prophet who has been getting these visions. Four chariots at once is a lot of traffic for one pair of mountains, and I bet he stood there with his mouth open.

Olive trees do show up in Zechariah's visions, but that's a different night. In Zechariah 4:3 he sees two olive trees beside a lampstand. This time, what comes out from between the two mountains is "four chariots," and the mountains are made of bronze. Easy to mix up, friend, because the man sees a LOT of things.

You're thinking of another vision, friend. Zechariah sees a flying scroll earlier, in Zechariah 5:1. This one is different: "four chariots coming out from between two mountains—mountains of bronze." That's two visions with one man staring at the sky, and I can see why they blur together.

Yes, baker. The text says the horses were red, black, white and dappled, "all of them strong." Not one weak team in the bunch. Not a single tired horse hoping nobody would notice. That's a lineup I'd be proud to have in my bakery.

The text says the opposite. After naming the red, black, white and dappled horses, it adds "all of them strong." Every team, no exceptions. I get why you might wonder, since four teams is a lot to keep track of, but none of them is the weak one.

explanations.answer: Asks the angel what they are
explanations.explanation: That's right. Zechariah says to the angel who was speaking with him, "What are these, my lord?" He doesn't pretend to understand and he doesn't wander off. He just asks. I wish I had done more of that in my own early days, instead of nodding at everything like I knew what was going on.

Zechariah doesn't chase anything, friend. The text says he inquired of the angel who was speaking with him: "What are these, my lord?" (Zechariah 6:4). He stays put and asks for the meaning. Chasing four chariots on foot sounds like a great way to get very tired and learn very little.

The text never says Zechariah takes notes. What it does say is that he asked the angel who was speaking with him, "What are these, my lord?" He wanted the meaning, not just the picture. A pencil would have been nice, but a question got him the answer.

Right on the money, baker. The angel says, "These are the four spirits of heaven, going forth from their station before the Lord of all the earth." So they start out standing in the Lord's presence. That tells you who they answer to.

Close to the right neighborhood, but not what the angel says. He says they go forth "from their station before the Lord of all the earth." The temple courts aren't mentioned in these verses. The chariots come out from between two bronze mountains, and the spirits stand before the Lord.

Shinar does show up in Zechariah's earlier vision, friend. In Zechariah 5:11 a house is built for the woman in the basket in the land of Shinar. But here the angel says the four spirits go forth "from their station before the Lord of all the earth." That's a very different address.

You've got it, baker. The angel says, "the one with the dappled horses toward the south." Black horses go north, white horses go west, and dappled horses go south. That's three directions out of four, and the red horses' direction isn't spelled out in these verses.

East isn't in the angel's directions. He says the black horses go toward the north, the white horses toward the west, and the dappled horses "toward the south." No east in sight, friend. Don't feel bad, though. Four teams and four compass points will make anybody's head spin.

North belongs to the black horses, not the dappled ones. The angel says, "The one with the black horses is going toward the land of the north." The dappled horses head "toward the south." Easy to swap them, baker, since they're all in the same sentence rushing past each other.

The text says the opposite. The horses are eager to go, and the LORD says, "Go and patrol the earth." Then "they patrolled the earth." No waiting around at the mountains. When the word comes, they go.
Yes, baker. No waiting happens here. The horses were "eager to go and patrol the earth," and the LORD said, "Go and patrol the earth." So they patrolled the earth. When the Lord says go, they go.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, "those going to the land of the north have given rest to My Spirit in the land of the north." He's the one speaking, so it's His Spirit. That's the end of this night vision, and the end of Zechariah's six visions in this group, but the book of Zechariah isn't over yet.

Zechariah isn't the one who owns this spirit, friend. He is the one being spoken to. The LORD summons him and says those going north "have given rest to My Spirit in the land of the north." The word is "My," and the LORD is the one speaking.

The angel has been doing the explaining, so I see why you'd guess him. But in verse 8 it's the LORD who speaks. He summons Zechariah and says, "those going to the land of the north have given rest to My Spirit in the land of the north." So it's the LORD's Spirit.
